set.note: From German Leitmotiv, 'leading motive.' The term became famous through Wagner's operas, though Wagner himself did not use it.

why: Note falsely says the word was first used for Wagner's operas; first printed use was by F. W. Jähns (1871) about Weber, and Wagner never used the term.

set.def: grossly unfair and morally wrong; wicked

why: 'especially in a way that harms the weak' is not part of the word's meaning (WordNet/dictionaries: wicked, grossly unfair); over-specified def misleads.
'facetiously' fits the cloze (joking remark about seeing the sunrise) and ex1 equally well.
'spoke scathingly/sardonically of it' fits the cloze; scathingly's def overlaps (critical).
'spoke disparagingly of the company's conduct' fits the cloze; defs overlap.
Near-synonym (calm, not easily upset); fits the cloze and overlaps for def questions.
'strongly castigate the use of antibiotics' is plausible in the cloze; both mean express strong disapproval.
rigmarole also means a confused, meaningless string of statements (WordNet sense 1); 'a rigmarole of contradictory times' fits the cloze.
braggadocio can also mean a braggart; 'exposed as a braggadocio' after bragging fits the cloze.
Defs overlap (risible includes 'so poor'); 'the excuse was frankly execrable' fits the cloze.
'an avaricious practice' (price gouging) and 'an execrable practice' both fit the cloze sensibly.
A censorious (fault-finding) hall monitor scolding students fits the cloze.
'a supercilious wave of her hand' dismissing a question fits the cloze.
Calling a cramped closet 'charming' so we trust him less also fits a mendacious realtor.
A crotchety or supercilious (scornful) critic finding fault with every film fits the cloze.
'answered sardonically, with a quick joke' is a sensible fill of the cloze.
'glibly replied' with a jokey answer fits the cloze sensibly.
'tried to beguile Grandpa into buying the warranty' fits the cloze.
beguile also means to deceive/cheat ('beguile someone out of'); could fit the cloze.
'The iniquitous business partner' (wicked) could sensibly fill the betrayal cloze.
'tendentious testimony' (deliberately slanted) could plausibly fill the cloze.
'sat crotchety at her desk, refusing every attempt to cheer her up' is plausible.
Both mean see-through/transparent; 'a limpid veil' is a possible reading.
A peremptory owner refusing to delay despite the engineers is a plausible fill.
'obdurate pride made her ignore all advice' is a plausible fill.
'was peremptory all day, snapping at anyone' is a plausible fill.

set.note: Usually describes a person's polished manner; it can also mean the quality of city life.

why: Note 'Describes manner, not cities' is false: urbanity also means urban character/city life (WordNet sense 2).

ex: The judge said the fraud, which targeted elderly widows, showed real moral turpitude.
The scandal revealed a level of turpitude that shocked even longtime cynics.

why: ex1 (contracts allow firing for moral turpitude) nearly duplicated the cloze sentence, giving the answer away.

ex: The old neighborhood is a palimpsest of faded signs, painted-over murals and new cafés.
After decades of amendments, the town charter had become a palimpsest, with traces of every old rule still visible.

why: ex2 used only the literal manuscript sense (the 'also' sense), not the defined figurative sense.
'trinket' is a small ornament, not a synonym for an unimportant matter.
'fiasco' means a complete failure, not a confused, complicated situation.
'overwhelming' does not mean impossible to overcome.
